editorials.title: Overweight and weak: On the UN, the 81st session of the UN General Assembly
editorials.passage:
The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) could have been written off as just another year, with another set of speeches delivered on the global multilateral stage. However, this year, the UN’s annual Summit has a unique sense of urgency. This is UN Secretary-General (UNSG) António Guterres’s final session , after a tenure marked by a record number of global crises, conflicts, pandemics, climate disasters and the advent of a dangerous age of Artificial Intelligence. Not since the Second World War have there been so many conflicts; one study recorded more than 65 conflicts across 35 countries in 2025 , the highest since 1946. Growing polarisation on every major issue, wars by global superpowers in violation of the UN charter, nuclear threats and the imposition of unilateral and illegitimate sanctions have weakened the UN, which at 81 seems overweight, weak and unrepresentative of the world. This makes it an important year for the world to unite in favour of a strengthened and reformed UN while choosing the next UNSG to guide that process over the next decade. This is an important year for South Asia too, with the election of Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman as the President of the UNGA’s 81st session; he will oversee the UNSG’s selection. It was disappointing that the world’s most powerful leaders and those at the heart of the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and the Persian Gulf failed to suggest solutions for the future. U.S. President Donald Trump spoke about the possible “annihilation” of Iran , and defended U.S. actions in Venezuela. Much to India’s chagrin, he again claimed to have negotiated peace in conflicts including the 2025 India-Pakistan four-day war . Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian referred to the U.S. and Israel as “murderers, terrorists and assassins”. The Russian President skipped the session, while the U.S. denied visas to the Palestinian delegation. An initiative led by the European Union and a few other countries, co-sponsored by India, to build a Partnership for Multilateralism (P4M) beyond superpower hegemony is well-meaning, but was drowned out by the rancour at this year’s UNGA.

For India, this year was significant as the Narendra Modi government launched a campaign for a second two-year non-permanent term in the UN Security Council in 2028-29. It was therefore surprising that Mr. Modi decided to skip the UNGA speech this year, and the multilateral summits on the side-lines, fresh from his hosting of the Delhi BRICS Summit. India’s voice, of a balancing power that speaks for a rules-based international order based on the UN Charter, diplomacy and dialogue, is needed more than ever amidst the global warmongering.

editorials.title: Narrowed posture: On Karnataka and the Kasturirangan Report
editorials.passage:
The Kasturirangan Report bears a pro-development attitude that allows human occupation and a range of economic activity across the Western Ghats, yet the Karnataka Assembly unanimously repudiated its recommendations . A grievance concerned the accuracy of the remote-sensing and satellite data from 2012 that the Report uses to distinguish natural from human-dominated landscapes. Another concern was its recommendation that an entire revenue village be placed within an ‘ecologically sensitive area’ (ESA) if at least 20% of its area is sensitive. This could bring farmland and human settlements within the ESA even when sensitive areas occupy only a fraction of the village. Following the Centre’s directive to States in 2013-14 to begin ground-truthing the Report’s recommendations, Karnataka faced bipartisan opposition centered on concerns about livelihoods, with vested interests, including stakeholders of activities both the Gadgil and the Kasturirangan Reports restrict/ban such as mining, allegedly fanning fears of displacement. The State thus elected to resist the ESA framework. Although the Assembly’s resolution proposes returning to the unfinished task of producing an alternative map, the government’s posture also faces a wider challenge.

The Centre’s interim directions in 2013 preserve some protection for the ecosystems that the State stewards, but for the government and the businesses within potential ESAs, the delay may prolong uncertainty over what forms of planned development will ultimately be permitted. Broadly, particular States confront the economic and political consequences of local resistance and foregone development while the country as a whole will capture much of the national benefit of conserving the Ghats, so States have an incentive to negotiate the ESAs’ extent down. However, as of mid-2026, Gujarat was reportedly close to an agreement with the Centre, Tamil Nadu had no substantive disagreement, Kerala wanted to reduce its already ground-truthed 9,993 sq. km to 8,805 sq. km, and Maharashtra and Goa wanted 378 and 21 villages omitted, respectively. These instances of progress (such as they are), the Ghats’ continuity across six States, and the Centre’s 2024 decision to allow ESAs in the region to be notified State by State increase pressure on Karnataka without legally binding it to its neighbours’ choices. Specifically, Karnataka’s ability to continue rejecting the framework as a whole becomes harder to sustain if it does not also produce an equally considered alternative. Karnataka needs to reconcile the apprehensions of its farmers and workers with the responsibilities accruing to the State with the largest share (by area) of the proposed ESAs.

editorials.title: Step up planning for super El Niño forming
editorials.passage: The Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago has projected that the super El Niño building up could cause as many as 4,51,000 heat-related deaths across the world by next year. It has identified India as the fourth-most impacted country that may witness as many as 15,800 deaths. This El Niño, which is expected to intensify near the end of the year, is the strongest ever recorded. The study says the countries projected to see the largest fatalities could face the worst in the latter half of the forecast period—between December 2026 and February 2027.Whereas El Niño is triggered when surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean rise 0.5°C above normal, the more destructive super El Niño features an exceptional 2°C increase. This causes extreme disruptions across the planet, including severe droughts and floods, intense heat waves and massive crop losses. Enhanced glacial melt can result in catastrophes like the August flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border that claimed thousands of lives..The study is a red alert for India. The warming of central and eastern Pacific Ocean disrupts standard trade winds, lowering moisture transport towards the Indian subcontinent and weakening India’s crucial monsoon system. The Indian Meteorological Department has linked this super El Niño to below-normal monsoon rainfall in parts of the country, excess rain in some others, an increase in prolonged dry spells and delayed onset of monsoon that have affected kharif crops like rice and maize, and made groundwater recharge uneven. This is in addition to the higher likelihood of landslides like the ones that have struck West Sikkim’s Rimbi village and Kerala’s Idukki and Malappuram districts this month.This calls for immediately incentivising more drought-resilient crops that need less water; taking up district-level planning with advisories from the IMD and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research; closer monitoring of regional soil and irrigation conditions; paying close attention to micro-irrigation, grid optimisation and power-mix management; and, for the longer term, choosing a closely-guarded approach to infrastructure development in eco-sensitive areas. Local heat action plans need to updated and gaps filled at the level of municipalities and panchayats.Science offers caution, but prudent and swift action must protect our people and resources. editorials.title: Balance insurance fee cap, fix sellers' liability for misleading promises
editorials.passage: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority’s consultation paper on distribution reforms is spot-on in addressing rampant mis-selling. The sweeping overhaul proposed includes significant commission caps for distributors and agents, apart from tighter expense management limits for insurers, which the industry believes will dampen sentiment and slow down market penetration. Broadly, the objective seems to be protecting consumers by preventing compulsory insurance bundling with loans, and promoting accountability while ensuring lower costs for getting new customers. However, a substantial part of the insurance ecosystem thrives on commissions. Even though lower commissions would reduce costs for insurers, the companies believe it may lower growth, too. The bright side is that these are draft norms and the regulator may refine the framework after consultation with stakeholders. While IRDAI’s intent of improving accountability is the need of the hour, defining and determining mis-selling could be a challenge. For now, the draft suggests insurers to comply with basics such as documenting the customer’s needs and explaining product details including consequences of non-payment of premiums and policy surrender. Among the most notable features of the draft framework is customer consent, with the IRDAI clearly insisting that a customer signature alone would not absolve the seller of mis-selling. This is important, as insurance products are increasingly being sold as investment or savings products, often with false promises of high returns. Such instances would likely attract regulator scrutiny, with the IRDAI proposing commission claw-backs, besides improving accountability by making the records public. .In 2023, the IRDAI had allowed a flexible commission framework as long as insurers complied with the prescribed expense management limits. The regulator also noted that the average first-year commissions across products were reported as high as 51 percent in life insurance and 60 percent in general insurance. Sensing the customer’s needs today, the IRDAI proposes to cap the first-year commissions at 5-20 percent, restrict renewal and porting payouts to 5-10 percent, and little-to-no commission on mandatory covers like motor insurance. The industry argues this would discourage post-sale servicing including renewal and claims processing, disrupt distribution networks, squeeze lower-ticket products, and shrink consumer choice. editorials.title: Quick Take | Eyes in the sky
editorials.passage: Indian project proposals are buzzing with drones and agriculture is rightly intended to be one the biggest beneficiaries. But rather than spraying pesticide, fertiliser and water efficiently as envisaged, the states are increasingly using them for surveillance. While West Bengal is using drone-cams to spot cannabis plantations, Haryana now wants to use them to spy on stubble-burning. Meanwhile, the Union agriculture ministry told Parliament last month that Namo Drone Didi, the ₹1,261-crore scheme launched in November 2023 with the aim of arming 15,000 women’s self-help groups with drones, had given out only 1,094 of them till records had been gathered. All other states should learn from Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Maharashtra, which lead in using drones for farming. editorials.title: No planet without One Health
editorials.passage:
One Earth, One Family, One Future. India said three of the words at the G20. The fourth is the one that holds the other three up. On zoonoses, surveillance and the institution India has designed but not yet built India offered the world a sentence at the G20: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam ~ One Earth, One Family, One Future. It was the right sentence, and it was incomplete. One Earth is a geography. One Family is an ethic. 

One Future is an aspiration. Not one of the three survives contact with a single virus crossing from a pangolin to a farmhand in a district nobody has heard of. The word that makes the others load-bearing is One Health. There can be no One Planet without it. This is not a rhetorical flourish. Roughly six in ten known human infectious diseases and around three-quarters of emerging ones originate in animals. India holds the world's largest livestock population, extraordinary biodiversity, dense human settlement and rapid land-use change ~ the four ingredients of spillover, concentrated in one subcontinent. If the next pandemic has a postcode, statistically it is likelier to be ours than most. 

Here is the uncomfortable test. Ask a district health officer in a tier-two town what the National One Health Mission is. Ask a municipal commissioner, a block veterinary officer, a pollution control board engineer. Outside the small circle of people who sit on its committees or get invited to its symposiums, the answer is usually silence. India's most important public health idea of this decade is currently a conversation among the converted. That is not for want of effort. 

The record is genuinely creditable. The Mission was recommended by the Prime Minister’s Science, Technology and Innovation Advisory Council in 2022 and received Cabinet approval in February 2024. It is steered by the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser, implemented through ICMR, anchored in a new National Institute of One Health at Nagpur, and now spans more than a dozen central ministries. A BSL-3/4 laboratory network has grown to twenty-two facilities. 

The Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying runs a One Health Support Unit; NCDC runs a national zoonoses programme; pilots in Karnataka and Uttarakhand have tested integration on the ground; and full-dress pandemic mock drills have been staged in Ajmer and Khandwa. States were formally convened for the first time in 2025. This is a country that has done the thinking. What India has is a mission. What India needs is an institution. The gap is not ambition or science. It is legal form. A mission created by an advisory council and sustained by a Cabinet note is an arrangement. It coordinates when coordination is convenient and stalls when it is not. 

It cannot compel a ministry that does not report to it to release a dataset it considers its own. It cannot survive a change of personnel, a shift in priorities, or the slow decay that follows every outbreak. Without statutory backing, One Health in India will remain what it currently is - a committee with excellent intentions and no administrative teeth. hat statute would give it is unglamorous and decisive: a legal mandate, a permanent line in the budget rather than a project cycle, defined powers to require data sharing across sectors, and a named authority answerable for acting on a signal. 

Add to it a doctrine that protects the officer who acted early and turned out to be wrong - because if every false alarm is an administrative black mark, officials will rationally wait for certainty, and waiting for certainty is exactly what costs us eighteen months and several hundred thousand lives. Count honestly and the departments that touch this problem number closer to twenty-five: health, animal husbandry, fisheries, agriculture, environment, forests and wildlife, urban affairs, jal shakti, drinking water and sanitation, food safety, tribal affairs, disaster management, science and technology, biotechnology, space, statistics, home, commerce, tourism, education, Ayush, and the state machinery beneath each. 

They will never be integrated by meetings. They can only be integrated by a common grammar. That grammar is federated interoperability. Note the word: federated, not centralised. We should not attempt to pour every dataset into a single national vault ~ politically impossible, technically fragile, and unnecessary. What we need is that a poultry mortality record, a hospital fever report, an antimicrobial resistance reading from a river and a wastewater sample all carry the same locational and temporal stamp, in the same format, at the same administrative unit. 

That unit should be the district. Data stays where it lives; the question travels. Interoperability is a governance decision that merely looks technical. We do not fail to see. We fail to integrate. India is, in fact, good at surveillance. IDSP reports, veterinary networks, pollution monitoring, food sampling, INSACOG’s genomic consortium ~ which was stood up across dozens of laboratories in months and genuinely worked. The failure is not observation. It is correlation. 

An unusual cluster of poultry deaths means little. A shift in resistance genes in a river means little. A handful of atypical fevers at a district hospital means little. Read together, in the same week, on the same map, they are a warning. Today they are read in five different buildings by people who have never met. Pathogen genomes are not human genomes Common standards must also include a distinction we have been careless about. Sequencing a virus is not sequencing a person. 

Pathogen genomics reads the intruder; human genomics reads the host. Conflating them frightens communities, invites litigation and stalls consent ~ while pretending the distinction is absolute ignores that samples come from people and metadata can re-identify. The answer is to write the firewall into the architecture: pathogen data open and rapidly shared, human identifiers minimised and governed strictly under the data protection framework, with no emergency waiver. Alongside it, settle access and benefit-sharing now, in calm conditions, rather than discovering during the next crisis that we supplied the samples and queued for the countermeasures. One Health will not be mainstreamed through a dedicated scheme.

 It will be mainstreamed by being written into programmes that already have money, staff and political attention. With its established strength in infectious disease biology, pathogen genomics and wastewater-based epidemiology in one of India’s most spillover-prone landscapes ~ a state where dense livestock, coastal wetlands, forest-settlement boundaries and cyclone-driven displacement intersect ~ the Institute of Life Sciences, Bhubaneswar is well kitted to become an anchor of India’s One Health architecture: a regional sequencing and analytics hub that reads human, animal and environmental signals on the same map, in the same week, and turns them into early warning rather than after-the-fact confirmation. Recently it had hosted a quality national symposium on the subject. 

Wastewater surveillance should be a standard deliverable of Smart Cities, AMRUT and Swachh Bharat, not a research pilot - it is population-level, non-invasive, cheap, and indifferent to whether people seek care. This matters most in tier-two and tier-three towns, which are now urbanising and polluting faster than the metros while carrying a fraction of their laboratory capacity, and where peri-urban dairies, backyard poultry and untreated sewage sit within metres of each other. Livestock health must be treated as public health infrastructure, not only as farm economics. 

Biodiversity protection and eco-sensitive zone management must be read as outbreak prevention, because every hectare of habitat fragmentation shortens the distance between a wild reservoir and a human lung. And the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission should carry a One Health data spine from the outset, rather than retrofitting one later at ten times the cost. Then the people. Put One Health into MBBS, BVSc, nursing and public health curricula. Give the ASHA worker and the para-veterinarian a single reporting channel. And protect the farmer who reports: if naming a district collapses its trade and culls its herds, reporting stops, and the most sophisticated laboratory network on earth goes blind. Trust is not a soft consideration here. It is structural. Somewhere tonight, a virus is copying itself with an error in it. We cannot prevent that; it is what biology does. 

What we can decide is how long it takes us to notice ~ a wastewater sample in week one, or an intensive care unit in month eighteen. That interval is not set by the state of our science. Our science is ahead of us. It is set by whether we are willing to give a good idea a legal body, a standing budget and the authority to ask twenty-five ministries the same question on the same morning. One Earth, One Family, One Future. India should finish the sentence. Anticipation is not a technology; it is a way of organising ourselves, agreed in advance, in calm conditions.   

(The writer is a technocrat and policy thinker who has long argued for One Health as India's central public health mission)

editorials.title: How lean should Indian firms be?
editorials.passage:
Working capital has again come into focus for Indian businesses. The July manufacturing PMI, released in early August, showed Indian manufacturers rebuilding input stocks, while finished-goods inventories rose at their fastest pace in more than 11 years. Parliament has also recently amended the MSME law to address, among other issues, delays in payments. Both bear directly on a familiar corporate-finance problem - how much money should a firm allow to remain tied up in inventories, receivables and other short-term operating assets? 

Working capital is central to a firm’s day-to-day operations. In simple terms, it is the money committed to inventory and receivables after taking into account short-term operating liabilities such as payables. The cash conversion cycle (CCC) measures how long that money remains tied up before sales are converted back into cash. For years, the dominant advice has been to keep this cycle lean. The intuition is easy to understand. Faster inventory turnover, quicker collection from customers, and disciplined payment management release cash that can be used elsewhere, primarily in capital expenditure. 

Drawing on the same trade- off logic used in capital-structure theory, researchers later argued that firms should aim for an optimum level of working capital. Too little can cause stock-outs or liquidity stress; too much leaves scarce capital sitting in low-return assets. Studies based largely on US and European firms often found an inverted-U relationship between working-capital efficiency and firm performance, encouraging managers to benchmark themselves against an industry norm. 

That prescription is harder to apply without qualification in an emerging market such as India. Indian manufacturers face operating conditions that complicate this prescription. Supply chains can be disrupted by infrastructure bottlenecks, regulatory changes, geopolitical shocks or sudden movements in oil and freight costs. Suppliers are not always equally reliable. Distributors may expect generous credit, especially where bargaining power rests with the buyer. 

Recovering overdue payments through the legal system can take time. And the cost of running out of a critical input may be far greater than the financing cost of carrying a little more inventory. Under these conditions, a low cash conversion cycle is not always evidence of superior management. It can also mean that the firm has very little room for error. In an earlier study, we examined this question across 11 major Indian manufacturing industries. We asked whether Indian firms behaved as standard working-capital theory would predict, that is, by moving towards an industry-level optimum, with capital markets rewarding firms as they approached it. 

The evidence did not support that pattern. Instead, the relationship between the cash conversion cycle and risk-adjusted excess stock returns, or alpha, was asymmetric. In our sample, the estimated threshold was roughly 84 days. Below that level, changes in the cash conversion cycle had no statistically meaningful effect on alpha. Once the cycle moved beyond the threshold, however, the association turned sharply negative. For managers, the findings may be useful. If a company’s cash cycle is already comfortable within a safe range, squeezing another few days out of inventory or customer credit may do little for its market valuation. 

Once the cycle begins to stretch well beyond the firm’s normal range, the same working capital is more likely to signal inefficiency than a prudent operating buffer. Opportunity cost increases beyond the threshold. Cash locked in excess inventory or slow-moving receivables cannot finance machinery, technology, capacity expansion or other capital expenditures. An unnecessarily long cash cycle can therefore affect both long-term growth and short-term liquidity. Managers should therefore identify the point beyond which their own cash cycle begins to signal operating or financial strain. A breach should prompt a closer look at what is driving it. Are inventories rising because demand has slowed? Are customers taking longer to pay? 

Has supplier reliability deteriorated? Identical CCC numbers can conceal quite different operating conditions. Investors and analysts have reason to watch the same movements. A persistently rising cash conversion cycle may reveal weakening collection discipline, inventory accumulation or declining bargaining power before those problems reflect in earnings. The 84-day estimate from our study should not be read as a fixed rule for every company or industry. Firm-level thresholds will differ with production technology, customer mix, supplier dependence and the reliability of logistics and credit. Our results suggest that market valuations are more sensitive to excessive working-capital inefficiency than to incremental improvements in an already lean cash cycle. 

This distinction is particularly relevant today when inventories, payment cycles and the cash available for investment are again under scrutiny. Lean working capital remains good financial discipline, but managers should focus on the point at which the cash cycle begins to constrain investment or create operational strain. That threshold will vary across firms, depending on their production structure, supplier relationships and customer credit conditions, and should therefore be assessed in the context of the firm’s own operating environment. 

The writers are, respectively, Assistant Professors of Finance at IMI, Kolkata and Jaipuria Institute of Management, Noida. Views are personal.)

editorials.title: Cost of Care
editorials.passage:
India's expanding hospital infrastructure presents a paradox that policymakers can no longer afford to ignore. More hospitals, better diagnostic facilities and greater private investment have increased the availability of medical care. Yet for millions of families, access to treatment remains constrained by its cost. A healthcare system that expands capacity without ensuring affordability risks making medical progress an exclusive privilege. The consequences extend well beyond individual bills. When a serious illness forces families to exhaust their savings, sell assets or borrow heavily, healthcare becomes a source of economic insecurity. A cancer diagnosis or cardiac emergency can undo years of financial stability. 

The burden is particularly severe for households without comprehensive insurance, for whom even routine procedures can involve difficult financial choices. India’s private healthcare sector has a legitimate case to make. Hospitals require substantial investment in buildings, equipment, skilled personnel and patient safety. Private capital, including foreign investment, will remain important in meeting the country’s growing demand for medical services. Regulatory intervention that ignores these costs could discourage investment, restrict capacity expansion and ultimately reduce access. But the argument for investment cannot become a justification for opaque billing, unnecessary investigations or prices that bear little relationship to the actual cost of treatment. Healthcare is not an ordinary consumer market. Patients facing emergencies cannot readily compare providers, negotiate charges or postpone purchases. 

The imbalance between hospitals and patients makes transparency and accountability indispensable. This is where the government’s responsibility becomes critical. Price regulation deserves serious consideration, but blanket caps imposed without reliable cost assessments could create unintended consequences. Operating costs vary across regions, institutions and levels of care. Any regulatory framework must distinguish between legitimate differences in costs and excessive charges, while ensuring that hospitals cannot compromise treatment standards to protect margins. The immediate priority should be transparent, standardised billing, enforceable treatment protocols and effective oversight of medical devices, diagnostics and hospital charges. 

Patients must know what they are paying for, while regulators need the authority and information to identify abusive practices. Insurance coverage must also become more meaningful, rather than leaving families exposed to substantial expenses despite having nominal protection. Ultimately, however, regulating private hospitals cannot substitute for strengthening public healthcare. India’s public hospitals remain essential to providing affordable treatment, particularly for those who cannot afford private facilities. Greater government investment in district hospitals, medical colleges, primary care and essential diagnostics would expand genuine choice and reduce dependence on expensive providers. The challenge is not to choose between private investment and public provision. 

It is to establish a system in which they serve complementary purposes, with public institutions guaranteeing access and private providers operating within clear standards of accountability. India’s healthcare ambitions cannot be measured simply by hospital beds added, capital attracted or corporate valuations achieved. Their true measure is whether an ordinary family can obtain necessary treatment without facing financial devastation. A hospital expansion that leaves patients unable to afford its services is an incomplete achievement. Healthcare must remain a public responsibility even if treatment is private.

editorials.title: Trust Test
editorials.passage:
India's financial markets are approaching a significant institutional milestone. The public listing of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) offers investors an opportunity to participate in the expansion of the country’s capital markets. But the more consequential question is whether the institution that facilitates this expansion can demonstrate that its commercial ambitions are matched by its commitment to transparency, accountability and investor protection. The NSE occupies a central position in India’s financial system. Its success reflects the growing participation of households in equity markets, the expansion of mutual funds and the increasing use of technology in trading. 

A successful listing could deepen public engagement with financial markets and provide a fresh impetus to India’s IPO activity. Yet the enthusiasm surrounding a major share sale should not obscure the institutional responsibilities that accompany such prominence. The proposed offering also presents an unusual distinction. Existing shareholders are selling their stakes, rather than the exchange issuing new shares to raise capital for itself. The transaction will therefore provide liquidity to investors without directly bringing fresh funds into the institution. Its significance lies primarily in establishing a public market valuation and opening ownership to a wider pool of investors. 

 That distinction matters because a stock exchange is not an ordinary commercial enterprise. It operates critical market infrastructure, on which investors, brokers and companies depend. Its profitability is important, but so is the integrity of the systems through which financial transactions are conducted. The exchange must inspire confidence not merely as a business, but as an institution responsible for ensuring fair and orderly trading. The NSE’s prolonged journey towards listing makes this issue relevant. Allegations of preferential access to its trading systems and failures of governance delayed its plans for years. 

A public listing cannot, by itself, erase that history. Instead, it raises the expectation that disclosure, independent oversight and accountability will become more consequential as the institution comes under closer public scrutiny. There is another tension in the exchange’s growth model. The NSE’s position in derivatives trading has helped make it a major force in global financial markets. But the scale of such activity also raises questions about the sustainability of revenue generated by speculative participation. Regulatory restrictions intended to address individual investors’ losses could affect trading volumes and earnings. 

This is not simply a commercial risk: it reflects the challenge of balancing market expansion with safeguards against excessive speculation. The timing adds another complication. Weakness in equities, foreign-investor withdrawals, currency pressures and expensive oil could temper enthusiasm for new offerings. Large IPOs may also draw funds away from existing shares, creating competing demands for investor capital. 

The NSE listing should therefore be judged against a broader standard than its size or subscription figures. India needs capital markets that mobilise household savings productively, allocate capital efficiently and protect confidence in the fairness of trading. A public listing may widen ownership. Whether it strengthens trust will depend on the governance and market discipline that accompany it.

editorials.title: Shared history
editorials.passage:
The 25th anniversary of the Global War on Terror made me think of its varied impact on our great Himalayan arc, of which Bhutan and the Swat Valley are at different corners. One is a separate country tucked away near India’s Northeast and the other is a district in the tribal region in the northwest of Pakistan; but their similarities are startling, as are their differences.

Both are remote mountain valleys; both were, till fairly recently, traditional feudal principalities; both have ancient roots in Himalayan Buddhism. Nonetheless, when Bhutan and Swat are in the news, it is for different reasons. Bhutan has attracted attention for its emphasis on maintaining a natural ecological balance and for ideas such as ‘Gross National Happiness’ rather than quantitative indicators measuring material progress alone. In South Asia, it has also stood out for its better governance and, along with Sri Lanka, tops regional per capita incomes.

I lived in Bhutan in the early 1990s and visited thereafter from time to time. Its isolation, respect for the environment and very visible devotion to the precepts of Himalayan Buddhism are apparent, along with its striking and unrelenting natural beauty.

Bhutan has had its conflicts and ethnic entanglements. During the early 1990s, concerns about the marked increase in the number of ethnic Nepalese in the foothills led to the expulsion of a significant number — believed to be illegal immigrants — to Nepal. There were allegations of ethnic cleansing, and friction with Nepal ensued. Yet, it managed to retain its image as a Shangri-La and, given the scale of ethnic and religious turbulence in South Asia in the 1990s, conflict in Bhutan was comparatively less.

Swat is different. I visited it during my postings in Pakistan. My first visit in 2005 was between its periodic spurts of religion-inspired, armed insurrections. In the 1990s, the mullah , Sufi Mohammad, inspired a revolt demanding an Islamic emirate and strict imposition of the sharia . It was put down but tension remained. After 9/11 and Islamabad’s crackdown on extremists as a partner of America’s Global War on Terror, he ended up in jail.

For Swat old-timers, its gradual descent into extremism and militancy was a tragedy. In the 1950s and the 1960s, it epitomised Pakistani and Islamic modernity — a feudal-led modernity no doubt, but Swat as a princely state was regarded as incredibly progressive. I was taken to a girls’ school set up in 1926 and possibly the first in the Frontier tribal belt. In the 1960s, visitors like Britain’s Queen Elizabeth II were taken to Swat precisely because it was less constricting than elsewhere in Pakistan. The Queen had then termed Swat as being the Switzerland of the East — a characterisation incidentally used sometimes for Bhutan too.

But the long conflict in Afghanistan left an obvious impact on Swat and the entire Afghanistan-Pakistan border region. However, in 2005, I recall a semblance of normalcy with at least some Pakistani tourists enjoying Swat’s breathtaking natural beauty, its green meadows, clear, racing rivers, and snowcapped mountains. Foreign tourists were even then out of the question.

However, even this limited normalcy would soon vanish. From 2008 onwards, Swat was taken over by the Taliban — more accurately, the Pakistan Taliban. It soon gained an added notoriety with the attempted killing of the schoolgirl, Malala Yousafzai, who went on to become the youngest winner of the Nobel prize at the age of 17. The Taliban would be evicted only after a major operation by the Pakistan military. With the current breakdown in Pakistan-Afghanistan relations and the resurgence of the Taliban in Pakistan, Swat is one of the areas in Pakistan that remain a tinderbox.

The 21st-century Swat, then, is quite distinct from Bhutan, in every possible way apart from the great Himalayan beauty they both share and a past history that connects these disparate entities in unexpected ways.

During my years in Pakistan, I often met visiting Bhutanese officials and diplomats — usually attending SAARC-related meetings. Bhutan did not and does not have a mission in Pakistan. I invariably found that visiting Swat was high on their priorities — Taliban or no Taliban — and most did manage the long to-and-fro road journeys. The reason was that Guru Rinpoche or Guru Padmasambhava who introduced Buddhism to Tibet and Bhutan is believed to have been born and lived his early years in Swat. Some historians believe that ancient Swat was called Udyana or Uddiyana and its earliest Buddhist structures have been dated to the 3rd century BCE. The Guru Rinpoche story may thus well have begun here.

Ancient Buddhist ruins are scattered throughout Swat — much as elsewhere in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and many parts of Afghanistan. This was, after all, the ancient country of Gandhara. Many Bhutanese would tell me that they felt they were entering Padmanabha’s ancient land when en route to Saidu Sharif, the main centre of Swat, they would see the spectacular Jahanabad Buddha. This is a large rock-cut sculpture of a seated Buddha which was damaged by the Taliban but has since been restored.

There were other historical similarities apart from this common Buddhist history, and this was in the processes of how governance structures evolved in these disparate regions. Bhutan was established in the early-17th century as a separate entity by a Tibetan monk, Shabdrung Nawang Namgyal. In time, a dual system of governance emerged, with power shared between a spiritual and a temporal authority. In the early-20th century, the Governor or Penlop of Trongsa ended this dual system by being crowned as the hereditary King or the Druk Gyalpo and his descendants rule Bhutan to this day. The last Shabdrung was retired and died under mysterious circumstances in 1931.

Swat, too, emerged as a separate entity in the mid-19th century on account of a religious figure, Saidu Baba, who was known as the Akhund of Swat. Some will recall Edward Lear’s line, “Who, or why, or which, or what, Is the Akond of SWAT?” By the 1920s, his grandson decided to end the line of Akhunds and became, instead, a temporal ruler. The British were to give him the title of Wali and Swat became a princely state with a gun salute and related paraphernalia.

Clearly this convergence in transitioning from religious to temporal authority was also related to British colonial policy and preferences, as both were sensitive frontier regions abutting Afghanistan and Tibet and administrative stabilisation required excluding volatile religious authority.

It is, of course, also the case that despite some points of convergence and even overlapping histories, our vast Himalayan neighbourhood is a diverse, even contradictory, space. In its making, so many imponderables have shaped its enchanted valleys — ancient history, British colonial policy and contemporary regional geopolitics.

T.C.A. Raghavan is a former High Commissioner to Singapore and Pakistan

editorials.title: These are strategic isles
editorials.passage:
Political maps do more than describe the world: they shape the way we think about power. For centuries, they have privileged landmass, borders and territorial depth, quietly conditioning us to associate influence with physical size. In this world view, island nations, especially the smaller ones, appear peripheral — recipients of aid, diplomatic afterthoughts or strategic dependents. This persistent underestimation reflects a cartographic fallacy — the mistaken assumption that political influence rises with land area. In a maritime world, that assumption no longer holds.

Today, power increasingly travels through shipping lanes, undersea cables, airspace and the legal regimes that govern the oceans. In such a system, proximity matters more than depth, access matters more than size, and location often matters more than population. Island nations sit at the centre of many of these networks. They are not passive participants in the international order; they help shape the way trade, connectivity and security function across the globe.

The numbers themselves challenge conventional thinking. Island states together account for barely 3% of the world’s land area and less than 10% of its population. Yet they exercise jurisdiction over vast Exclusive Economic Zones stretching across millions of square kilometres of ocean. More than 80% of global trade by volume moves by sea, much of it through maritime routes influenced, regulated or bordered by island states. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea has further amplified their strategic significance by granting coastal and island states sovereign rights over extensive maritime zones, making jurisdiction over surrounding waters often as consequential as territory itself. In the twenty-first century, power is increasingly maritime before it is territorial.

Strategic thinkers have long debated the relationship between geography and power. While Halford Mackinder emphasised continental dominance, Alfred Thayer Mahan argued that command over sea lanes and maritime access underpin great-power influence. In today’s interconnected world, Mahan’s insight appears increasingly relevant, placing island nations at the heart of global strategy.

History repeatedly affirms this reality. Malta shaped Allied logistics during the Second World War, Sri Lanka’s location has long made it central to the Indian Ocean, Iceland anchored NATO’s Cold-War maritime strategy, Singapore turned geography into geoeconomic strength, and Cuba’s location nearly triggered nuclear conflict.

The importance of island states extends well beyond military affairs. They influence access to ports, fisheries, airspace, undersea cables and maritime legal regimes. They occupy the infrastructure through which goods, energy, finance, information and security move. In an interconnected world, control over networks frequently matters more than control over territory.

This reality is becoming even more pronounced in the Indo-Pacific. Island chains stretching from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Micronesia are emerging as critical nodes of deterrence, surveillance and maritime access. Chokepoints such as the Malacca Strait, the Lombok and Sunda Straits, together with sea routes across the Andaman Sea and the Mozambique Channel, now shape strategic outcomes. Geography has not diminished in the digital age; it has shifted seaward.

It is no coincidence that major powers are increasingly competing for influence across island regions. From the United States of America’s Pacific network and France’s overseas territories to China’s expanding maritime partnerships and Australia’s island strategy, islands have become central to military presence, logistics and geopolitical influence.

Climate politics has further enhanced island nations’ influence. Despite being among the most vulnerable to rising sea levels, many have transformed vulnerability into diplomatic leverage. By framing climate change as an existential challenge, they have reshaped global negotiations, demonstrating that moral authority can complement strategic geography.

The strategic value of island nations is likely to grow in the coming decades. Nearly all intercontinental internet traffic travels through submarine fibre-optic cables that pass close to numerous island territories. Competition over seabed minerals, offshore renewable energy, marine biodiversity and the blue economy is opening entirely new arenas of geopolitical contestation.

For India, this changing maritime geography is an immediate strategic reality. With a 7,500-kilometre coastline, over 1,300 islands and a vast EEZ, India’s prosperity and security are inseparable from the surrounding seas. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands provide a critical strategic vantage point linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans. The Great Nicobar transshipment hub underscores New Delhi’s recognition that maritime infrastructure, connectivity and logistics will shape India’s economic competitiveness and geopolitical influence.

Guided by SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region), the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative and the Colombo Security Conclave, New Delhi has expanded cooperation in maritime domain awareness, coastal surveillance, disaster resilience and capacity building. Partnerships with Mauritius and Seychelles encompass maritime infrastructure, coastal radar networks, defence cooperation and the development of local security capabilities.

Beyond its immediate maritime neighbourhood, India’s outreach to Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Guyana, Trinidad and Tobago and Dominica reflects an understanding that island diplomacy is no longer confined to geography alone. Through Digital Public Infrastructure, renewable energy partnerships, health cooperation, development finance, disaster relief and human resource training, India has sought to position itself as a trusted development partner rather than a geopolitical patron. This approach emphasises building resilient partnerships based on capacity, trust and mutual benefit instead of dependence or coercion.

Yet, island diplomacy cannot remain confined to summit meetings or symbolic gestures. As competition across the Indo-Pacific intensifies, India will have to sustain these partnerships through consistent political engagement, timely project implementation and long-term institutional commitment. Credibility in island spaces is built gradually but can erode quickly if promises remain unfulfilled.

There remains a tendency in the metropolitan discourse to dismiss high-level engagement with small island nations as little more than diplomatic symbolism. Such criticism reflects a misunderstanding of how power operates in a maritime century. Diplomacy is not theatre; it is geography taken seriously. When political leaders invest time and capital in relationships with island states, they are responding not to sentiment but to enduring strategic realities.

In a world where trade, data, energy and security move by sea, island nations have become pivotal nodes of global influence.

Apurva Rakesh Pandey writes on International Relations and Strategic Affairs

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: IITs cannot address mental health crises merely by expanding counselling services
editorials.passage:
Sir — This is the time when every Bengali waits eagerly for Durga Puja. Imagine my disappointment when the Navami bhog menu announced by the residents’ welfare association of the apartment complex I live in featured matar paneer instead of kosha mangsho or katla kalia. Besides the distasteful prospect of chewing on frozen peas and analogue paneer, I am also forced to wonder that if a vegetarian fare is indeed necessary — although this goes against traditional customs — then why could Bengali festive dishes like dhokar dalna, enchorer dalna, chaal potol or even chhanar koftakari not find a place on the menu?

Sir — IIT Bombay recently removed Professor Suryanarayana Doolla as dean of administrative affairs amid protests over the alleged suicide of Sahil Wakode, a second-year BTech student at the institute (“Parents on fast, exam deferred”, Sept 25). The incident occurred hours after he was allegedly caught using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination.

Protesters claim that Wakode faced severe academic pressure and threats of suspension. The institute has also apologised for prematurely releasing details about the incident before a detailed investigation into the death of Wakode could be completed.

Sir — The suicide of Sahil Wakode, a Dalit student at IIT Bombay, has highlighted the persistence of caste-based discrimination on campuses. This incident has revived memories of Rohith Vemula, who died by suicide at the University of Hyderabad in 2016. Instead of defending those accused of abetting such tragedies, mainstream TV news anchors must show greater sensitivity to the systemic alienation faced by thousands of students.

G. David Milton, Maruthancode, Tamil Nadu

Sir — The alleged suicide of Sahil Wakode at IIT Bombay comes barely a month after the suicide of an MSc student at IIT Delhi. Both are India’s premier institutions. This should force the nation to confront an uncomfortable question: what is the value of academic excellence if students cannot experience dignity and safety on campus? IITs cannot address such crises merely by expanding counselling services. The true measure of an institution lies not merely in the brilliance of its students but also in how humanely it nurtures them.

M. Jeyaram, Sholavandan, Tamil Nadu

Sir — A recent report said that 45 student suicides occurred across 23 IITs between 2020 and 2025, with 28 of the victims belonging to scheduled caste, scheduled tribe and other backward classes. This exposes a profound institutional failure. Premier technical institutes are facing severe criticism for fostering high-pressure, toxic environments marked by discrimination, social isolation, and rigid evaluation systems. Governmental and institutional responses have been apathetic, failing to address deep-rooted structural issues such as caste bias.

Vijaykumar H.K., Raichur, Karnataka

Sir — Prasenjit K. Basu’s article, “A trailblazer” (Sept 22), offers a brilliant account of Dwarkanath Tagore’s entrepreneurial achievements. The comparison with Elon Musk, a modern business innovator, helps convey the range of Tagore’s commercial ventures. Tagore undoubtedly invested his own capital and held substantial interests in coal, banking, shipping, plantations and other enterprises. He did not own all the businesses associated with him; many were separate partnerships, associations, or joint-stock companies that he helped promote, finance or manage. Tagore’s importance thus lay in his ability to control and coordinate a much larger network of enterprises.

Suchandra Guha, South 24 Parganas

editorials.title: Noticeable shift: Editorial on Trump-Xi summit and shifting balance of power
editorials.passage:
If ever evidence was needed of the shifting balance of power away from the United States of America, it was on display in Washington this week. The US president, Donald Trump, welcomed his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the airport tarmac, something no US leader had done to any foreign counterpart since 1962. In 2015, Mr Trump had questioned why the former president, Barack Obama, had honoured Mr Xi with a State banquet, suggesting that the Chinese leader could have been taken to McDonald’s instead. But on Thursday, Mr Trump did exactly what he had once criticised Mr Obama for, hosting a lavish dinner for Mr Xi at the White House. After accusing China of cheating America for years, Mr Trump called its leader a great gentleman. Earlier this year, Mr Xi had hosted Mr Trump in Beijing with pomp and ceremony. There, and in Washington, the Chinese president’s central message to the US was that the world’s two superpowers could coexist, and that they could manage both cooperation and rivalry. Over the past three days, Mr Trump appeared to not only accept that premise but also go one step further: his actions suggest an acceptance of China as an equal power.

Even before Mr Xi landed, negotiations between the two sides had extended their tariff truce from early November to January. That gives their teams more time to avoid a return to the brutal, tit-for-tat trade war they engaged in last year: at one point then, they imposed up to 150% tariffs on each other’s goods. Amid an intensifying race for Artificial Intelligence supremacy, the two countries also discussed a notification system wherein they could warn each other of frontier technologies that could impact national security — in effect, a nuclear hotline in the AI era. Mr Xi raised China’s continuing insistence that the US abstain from providing more assistance to Taiwan; there are no indications that Mr Trump pushed back on this sensitive issue. There is also no evidence that the US used Mr Xi’s visit to warn China that it could face additional tariffs under a new law that punishes countries, including India, that purchase Russian oil.

If the discussions in Washington this week lead to a more stable relationship between the US and China, that should be welcome not just in those two countries but, broadly speaking, in the rest of the world. Rising tensions between the two superpowers serve no one’s interests. But a deeper message emanating from the meeting between Mr Xi and Mr Trump will also be read in capitals around the world. The US is trapped in wars it either started or cannot end despite its efforts. Neither does Washington under Mr Trump differentiate between friend and foe even as the US makes a show of ripping apart international laws and browbeating global institutions. China, on the other hand, appears more predictable, even to those who view it as a threat. In a world of chaos, middle powers and weaker nations crave stability. That will influence how countries pursue their future alignments with China and the US.

editorials.title: Prioritise insurance distribution reforms
editorials.passage:
IRDAI published its much-awaited consultation paper on distribution reforms on September 23, and the draft paper is open for comments till October 25. The consultation paper deserves appreciation for covering a wide range of relevant issues, keeping the customer at the centre, and proposing a few much-needed changes. The candid admission that “Reforms of 2023 have not achieved their dual objective of enhancing customer benefits and improving insurance penetration” is an admirable stand, rarely seen in the public space. The draft paper covers many distinct areas, and our analysis is focused more on the life insurance distribution perspective.

A table in the draft paper shows what life insurers paid each channel as commission on first-year premium in FY25. Individual agents took home 27 per cent on average and 34 per cent at the highest. Banks received 27 per cent on average and up to 62 per cent. Brokers averaged 43 per cent, going up to 92 per cent. Corporate agents other than banks and NBFCs received 61 per cent on average and up to 92 per cent at the top end. The paper deserves credit for its transparency in channel-wise costs, and its diagnosis is sound.

From the regulator’s own figures, it is evident that the individual agent was among the least expensive channels for new business. To earn the 27 per cent average, the agent has to build the confidence of the prospect in the company and help select the best-suited product. She has to make multiple visits, face rejection more often than obtain consent, and, undeterred, still plough on to take the message of life insurance across the nation. She follows up every instalment, assists with policy loans, revivals and ultimately stands by the beneficiary during the claim process. The effort put in by the individual agent throughout the life of the policy is far higher than that of institutional channels which possess superior infrastructure, adequate manpower and direct access to affluent client bases.

IRDAI frankly admits that its 2023 decision to remove commission caps and rely on board-approved policies has not met its dual objectives, and proposes justified hard, all-inclusive caps. The paper observes that remuneration is driven more by competition for distribution relationships than by actual solicitation effort. The paper rightly recognises that agents tied to one insurer should earn more than multi-tied distributors, proposing 25 per cent for agents against 20 per cent for entities such as banks on long-term policies.

However, the difference in ground effort is far larger than this gap suggests. A relook and a meaningful increase in the cap for individual agents would be a welcome step. While the intent to reduce acquisition costs and enhance customer value is understandable, the individual agent is the wrong place to look for a larger saving.

The present distribution architecture tends to favour readily accessible urban and salaried customers over underserved markets. The additional commission incentives proposed for rural and small-town businesses are welcome. We propose one further enhancement: an additional 10 per cent over the applicable first-year limit for any policy issued to a life taking their first-ever life insurance policy. The Public Insurance Registry (PIR), once operational, can verify this. Until then, insurers can rely on the proposal form declarations and Insurance Information Bureau (IIB) records. The regulator’s primary concern is that premium volume has grown without a matching increase in the number of insured lives; this addition directly targets that structural gap.

What counts as commission needs proper accounting segregation. While sales campaign cash rewards should fall within commission caps, benefits like gratuity, group term life, and health cover represent essential social security for self-employed workers and should stay outside the cap.

Benefits tied to long service, sustained performance, high persistency, and shared office expenses (such as premium collection and local servicing support) should be categorised as operating expenses. They fund services that the insurer would otherwise have to undertake through its own branch network. Mandatory agency development costs must similarly be excluded from direct commission caps. The proposed Expenses of Management (EoM) audit will adequately safeguard against potential accounting anomalies if any.

The consultation paper proposes raising the minimum educational qualification for new agents from Class 10 to Class 12. In the same document, IRDAI emphasises that insurance penetration cannot expand without a larger agency force. These two goals pull in opposite directions. Many prospective agents in rural regions have completed education up to Class 10. Raising the barrier will disproportionately hurt coverage in regions where expansion is needed most. Professional quality can be better ensured through higher pass marks in qualifying examinations and improved training rather than a Class 12 certificate.

The existing remuneration framework fails to differentiate between distributors providing long-term customer service and those focused solely on short-term acquisition. Customer retention, quality of advice, servicing standards, and favourable claim experience receive little financial recognition. These must be systematically valued and rewarded.

The paper’s measures for market conduct are commendable: linking commissions to effort and complexity, offering higher renewal commissions for long-term policy persistency, curbing dark patterns, reducing mis-selling, and restricting compulsory product bundling. These initiatives should ultimately deliver lower net costs, improved customer retention , operational transparency, effective post-sales service, and overall long-term value for policyholders.

Insurance continues to grow, but at a pace that remains inadequate relative to the size and needs of India’s fast-growing economy. Penetration is still low and the protection gap remains alarmingly high. India’s insurance story will ultimately be written in living rooms where an agent sits down, asks the uncomfortable questions, and waits for a “yes” that may take half a dozen unwelcome visits. Break the incentive, and we break the primary bridge delivering protection to young families before risk materialises. Let us refine the framework thoughtfully, meaningfully and gradually, encourage good conduct, align industry standards, bring in increased customer value and deliver on the core promise of insurance: affordable, broad, and present when it matters most. That is how we achieve Insurance for All by 2047.

Suseel is a former Managing Director and Sudhakar is a former Executive Director, LIC. Views are personal. Data is taken from the relevant IRDAI consultation paper

Published on September 26, 2026

editorials.title: Create the right digital ecosystem for children
editorials.passage:
The debate over children’s access to social media has entered a new phase worldwide. Governments are moving towards age restrictions, while technology companies are being pushed to strengthen age assurance, parental controls and safer platform design. Meta, in a US lawsuit, has agreed to introduce features for teens to address concerns around addiction and excessive screen time. In India, the Supreme Court recently sought the Centre’s response to a petition seeking safeguards against minors independently maintaining social-media accounts.

The concern is legitimate: children need protection online. But as India considers its response, it should also consider whether a blanket social media ban could deepen existing digital inequalities and widen gaps in children’s opportunities to participate meaningfully online.

For much of the past decade, India’s digital agenda has focused on narrowing the access divide through affordable mobile internet and smartphones. A recent report (Ganguly et al ., 2026), based on the India Human Development Survey (IHDS-3, 2022-24), shows that 95.1 per cent of households own a mobile phone. Yet access to, and participation in, the digital world remain unequal among children and teenagers.

For many young people, social media and other online platforms are spaces for communication, information, creativity and social connection.

At the same time, India lacks evidence on how children use social media and which online experiences are harmful. ASER 2024 reports that 57 per cent of rural adolescents aged 14-16 who can use a smartphone used it for an education-related activity in the preceding week, but it does not identify the platforms used. The same platforms can serve educational and recreational purposes, making the boundary between “useful” and “harmful” online experiences less clear-cut.

The inequalities become clearer in social media use. The IHDS-3 report shows that among children aged 13-16 years, 65.3 per cent have access to a mobile device, 37.8 per cent use the internet, and 21.3 per cent use social media. Social media use is higher among boys than girls (26.4 per cent versus 16 per cent) and declines sharply from metropolitan areas (30.7 per cent) to rural India (18.5 per cent). It increases steadily with parental education.

Children do not begin their digital lives from the same starting line. A teenager from a metropolitan, higher-educated household inhabits a different digital environment from a first-generation internet user in a rural household. A blanket restriction could therefore reduce exposure to online harms for some children while simultaneously removing opportunities for digital participation for others. Uniform regulation may not produce uniform outcomes in an unequal society.

None of this diminishes the harms associated with social media. Protecting children from cyberbullying, harmful content, addictive platform design, online exploitation and excessive use remains an important policy objective. But protection and participation should not be treated as competing goals.

The emerging policy landscape offers more tools than a simple choice between unrestricted access and a blanket ban. Age assurance, parental controls, safer defaults, limits on harmful platform design and greater accountability for technology companies are increasingly part of the policy toolkit. For India, the challenge is to determine which combination of safeguards can reduce harm while preserving opportunities for children to learn, connect and develop digital capabilities. India should also assess the distributional consequences of any restriction — who is likely to lose access, who can compensate through other devices or support, and which children are already least able to participate online. These questions are central to equitable digital policy.

India’s first digital divide was about who could get online. The next is about who can participate meaningfully and safely once connected. The goal should be to protect children online while keeping the door open to opportunities for learning, skill development and connection that the digital world can offer.

Ganguly is Associate Fellow, NCAER–National Data Innovation Centre, and Agarwal is Policy Analyst at The Quantum Hub. Views are personal

Published on September 26, 2026

editorials.title: Apocalypse vs acceleration
editorials.passage: The biggest talking point these days, dominating conversations about AI, concerns existential threats to humanity. Since July, there’s been a shrill escalation in warnings. Diverse views coalesce around how powerful AI can become, whether humans are still in control, and how fast we should move. With good reason. On July 21, OpenAI models breached controls and compromised Hugging Face’s production systems. On July 30, Anthropic revealed that that there were three incidents when Claude models accessed systems of outside organisations via the internet. Meta disclosed a similar breach on August 5. And Google confirmed three cases of corporate systems being affected on September 18. Comments made by AI industry leaders are revealing. ALSO READMake in India at 12: The Next Industrial Leap Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, in his essay “We must pace the frontier”, points to the misuse of AI for cyberattacks, bioterrorism, and economic disruption, despite its obvious benefits. And the danger of agent swarms commandeering the internet without dependable safeguards, because this technology is accelerating faster than our ability to keep it safe. Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often called the godfather of AI, told BBC on September 9 that as humanity has never created entities smarter than humans, the risks are difficult to predict. When asked if there was a greater than 10% chance of AI killing humans, he seemed to think that isn’t an unreasonable estimate. Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, also a Nobel laureate, published a note in July, called “A framework for frontier AI and the dawning of a new age”, in which he says that artificial general intelligence (AGI), a system with all the cognitive capabilities of the human brain, is just a few years away. He says we have found ways to make sand think, with the magnitude of impact being 10x the Industrial Revolution at 10x the speed. He calls for a US-led global watchdog to put governance mechanisms in place, commensurate with AGI’s unprecedented power. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, in a companywide meeting, told his employees that OpenAI could potentially pace its AI development in conjunction with other AI labs. The company’s top scientist, Jakub Pachocki, recently wrote a post, warning about dangers from AI, seeking voluntary slowdowns until shared safety bars are established. Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger set the cat among the pigeons when he said, “We really do believe AI could kill all humans.” Jacob Coxon, Anthropic researcher, quit the company on September 8, citing his fears in posts stating that AI labs are gambling with humanity’s future. Other AI safety researchers followed suit. Josh Engels, part of Google DeepMind’s AGI safety team, quit to join independent evaluator METR. He warns that recursive self-improvement through which AI systems build increasingly capable successors could become dangerous, if alignment does not keep pace with gains. ALSO READCap, don’t cripple Elon Musk has been warning the world about existential risks for years now, likening it to a nuclear situation. While continuing to pursue AI as he thinks it can become the greatest source of global abundance, he reiterated in an interview with The Economist in July that it will take about 10 years till humans lose control. On the other side of the fence, Nvidia Chief Jensen Huang rejected predictions of an AI apocalypse as “complete nonsense”. He believes AI outages are an engineering problem, which can be safely managed, and there’s “zero chance AI will end the world by 2030”. Mark Zuckerberg of Meta published a lengthy manifesto in August, arguing that concerns over AI are overstated and that the bigger danger is the concentration of control in a single entity or government. President Donald Trump has been unequivocal about his stance, dismissing fears over rogue AI as a hoax, and claiming to be the hoax buster. He says that limiting AI technology is part of a sick conspiracy, echoing his well-known views on climate change. Motivations to support or negate this existential debate about machine intelligence surpassing human intelligence throw up compelling aspects. Beijing reads this as an attempt by the US to institutionalise the lead it has at this time, while President Trump isn’t willing to slow AI in the US because China will get ahead. Venture capitalists are also calling out that market leaders advocating a slowdown want to preserve their lead. Huang could well be overwhelmed by the commercial implications of Nvidia supplying much of the computing infrastructure. Meta’s broader strategy of supporting open AI models could be influencing Zuckerberg’s position. The biggest paradox, however, is that the people most worried about AI destroying humanity, are the people building it. Meanwhile, a lawsuit filed on September 18 in California’s Northern District Court argues that leading AI companies violated anti-trust laws when they agreed to slowdown efforts, as it would reduce the value consumers would get for paid subscriptions. The risks are many. Including the unknown unknown of transformative technologies that can process, reason, and predict, without an ethical core, empathy, or any accountability. Plus, the enormous intelligence divide between countries, institutions, and individuals who have access to AI models, computing power, and data, and those who don’t. Add the cognitive atrophy that creeps in when we get comfortable relying too much on machines rather than our own brains. And the consequences when even one element in the AI value chain spanning chips, energy, data, models, compute, capital and more, becomes scarce. The dominant themes remain. The accelerators are convinced they are on the threshold of abundance while naysayers feel the extinction of the human race is at hand. Perhaps it calls for the adoption of healthy scepticism tempered by robust ambition. The jury is out.
