editorials.title: In his final UN speech, Macron may have given other leaders a valuable parting gift: the guts to stand up to Trump
editorials.passage:
O n the first day of the United Nations general assembly this week, two world leaders outlined competing visions for the future. Donald Trump’s speech was disturbingly familiar to those he’s given before: a litany of false boasts and odd tangents, peppered with grim military threats against a variety of nation states. Discussing his seven-month war with Iran, he mused over whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.

In Trump’s eyes, the world is there to be ruled – and ruled only by the US, whose economy is “the envy of the world” and military is “the most powerful on Earth”.

A couple of hours later, Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to offer an alternative. In a full-throated defence of international law, multilateralism and the rules-based order, the French president said we were living in a “new era of barbaric acts”. He directly criticised Russia and Israel, but much of it was clearly aimed at Trump. “They say might is right … but we will not yield,” he argued. “We cannot simply accept this new order of impunity which some are trying to erect … Do we want to live under … the law of the jungle or do we want to live in a civilised international society?”

Importantly, he also acknowledged the west’s “permanent temptation to espouse double standards”. “How many times have we heard that people’s sovereignty has value in Europe , but if we look at the Middle East and Africa, it is less valuable,” he asked. “No, that is unacceptable … A life is a life. Peace and security are indivisible, and everyone has a right to them.”

Over the past decade, Macron has consistently been one of the only western leaders with a morally intelligent analysis of what Europe and the world should look like. As Trump, Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu have ushered us into an age of impunity, he has defended the rules-based order and, in recent months, been at the forefront of attempts to forge new alliances to support the crumbling old ones.

He has pushed the idea of European strategic autonomy more than anyone else, understanding that while Europe is an economic power, it is yet to fully realise its potential as either a military or geopolitical force. During Trump’s first term, Macron was the only major leader willing to publicly acknowledge that Nato could no longer rely on the US, leaving the alliance all but dead.

And yet the big speeches have rarely led to any substantial change. His ambitious call for EU reform in 2017 went nowhere, in essence scotched by Angela Merkel , who praised his “passion” and “verve” but failed to back the substance. Likewise, in New York this week, while his analysis was sound, the solutions were slight.

This isn’t necessarily all Macron’s fault. He came to power in May 2017 as the new world order was crumbling. The EU was in crisis: one of its largest members had just voted to leave, while the remaining member states were still fatally split over the fallout from the eurozone crisis earlier in the decade and the migration wave in the summer of 2015. France’s two biggest European allies have been on the slide during his time in office. He has had to work with three German chancellors, the most recent two less popular than their predecessors, and is now on his sixth British prime minister.

More urgently, Trump had taken office four months earlier, signalling the start of the break up of the rules-based order that had guided the west since the end of the second world war. Had Macron had the chance to work with Barack Obama, Angela Merkel at the peak of her popularity and a British prime minister committed to the EU, things might have turned out differently.

Macron’s domestic woes have increased his impotence on the world stage. He has in effect been a lame duck for the past two years, since his disastrous snap election in 2024 left him without a majority.

But his speech in New York, his final UN address before he steps down as president next spring, may have a more lasting impact. It certainly set the tone for the week. Over the following days, a procession of leaders of the so-called middle powers defended the principles of the UN and offered coded criticisms of Trump. Many of those who would have been scared of speaking out last year feel more emboldened now.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, warned that “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone”, while Spain’s PM, Pedro Sánchez, said he sought to “defend what so many are trying to destroy” and called for countries to come together to fight “political actors and governments that want to take us back to a dark past”.

The middle powers are united in their opposition. The question is whether they can agree on what they’re for. The events of the past few weeks suggest that process is under way. New alliances based on values, not geography or size, are being formed – a reinvention of multilateralism, rather than a simple defence of the old model.

So far this month, the EU and Canada have discussed the idea of “associate membership” , while the UK has formed a new coalition of middle powers to impose sanctions targeting Israel’s unlawful occupation of the West Bank.

Another new group was created at the UN this week, with Finland and Norway launching a call for an international body to oversee the safety of AI models. It is a direct challenge to Trump, who has called concerns about AI safety a “hoax” – nonetheless, 27 world leaders signed up, including Macron, Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Albanese.

What ties all this together is the idea of “values-based realism”, an argument first put forward by the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, and echoed this week by Carney, who arguably lit the “middle powers” spark in Davos earlier this year when he spoke of the “rupture” in the world order caused by Trump. The new world Carney, Macron and others are trying to build will be one of different, sometimes overlapping alliances of like-minded states.

There will be an ongoing question here for Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband. Which of these groups do they join, which do they try to form themselves and which do they politely decline? Despite Burnham’s desire to lead the push for new global AI standards, the UK has so far not joined the Finnish AI group, perhaps for fear of invoking Trump’s wrath. Another issue emerged this week: how to respond to Trump’s desire to invite Putin to the G20?

Each middle power will face the same conundrum: when to fight back and when to sit on the sidelines. At least now the middle powers have understood that fighting back is an option.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

editorials.title: Amazon’s Ring wants to replace local WhatsApp groups. It’s a recipe for curtain-twitching disaster
editorials.passage:
R ing, the Amazon subsidiary of camera-enabled doorbells fame, wants to be an even bigger part of your neighbourhood. Next month in the UK, it will be launching Neighbours , a community app that seeks to replace the now traditional neighbourhood Facebook or WhatsApp group. It will be available inside the Ring app, free to everybody, including people without Ring products, and will include a community requests feature wherein the police can ask for footage from residents living near reported crimes, who can then choose whether or not to share it.

My first thought was that this is curtain-twitching culture gone mad. If you must have a Ring doorbell (and my instinctive feeling as someone without one, a feeling I will no doubt have until I get one and decide it’s great, is that it’s narc-coded behaviour) then: OK. But does Amazon need to be in charge of a digital village messageboard too?

The selling point, Ring thinks, is that posting will be anonymised, and posters will have to conform to strict guidelines on what they are allowed to post. It would, in other words, be very unlike the lawless badlands of a neighbourhood WhatsApp .

Maybe people really did want these groups replaced by something more centrally managed. I asked around people I knew about the WhatsApp communities that they were in, and the kinds of behaviour they had witnessed. Some of it, naturally, demonstrated an ugly dislike of homeless people, fear and loathing of door-to-door salespeople, racial profiling of local youths, and the view that everyone not personally known to the residents was a criminal in waiting.

Some of what people encountered on these groups was just strange: a north London WhatsApp group of more than 500 people having to disband because someone was giving away a Hewlett-Packard printer and another person said that shouldn’t be allowed because of BDS ; a woman forced to recuse herself from a neighbourhood group because she saw a toad get squashed by a car, and was inundated with local volunteers who wanted her to set up and run a toad protection squad in case there were other vulnerable toads in the area; a man with a vendetta against a local couple who were feeding the foxes that went on to rip up his garden taking to his local chat to respond with witty bons mots such as “they are as stubborn as the foxes themselves but lack their intelligence”; repeated reports about a “sick cat” that people familiar with the animal had to confirm was “just ugly”; and this is leaving out the party poopers, bin police and other assorted oddballs.

But then there were the wonderful stories, too: the organisation of a funeral procession for an older woman who died on the street with no immediate family; borrowing laptop chargers and camping equipment; taking in people who had locked themselves out. And all of these led me to feel a little envious.

I’ve just moved, but for four years before that I lived on a street in south London. One time, I witnessed something insane happen. My flatmate was at home one Saturday afternoon and heard an altercation on the street, and looked out the window to see what was going on. He was, in his way, curtain twitching. A neighbourhood cat, a friendly local celebrity who always greeted you as you passed, had been mauled to death by an XL bully being walked past the house where it lived.

The cat’s owners were, understandably, furious and upset. The noise my flatmate heard was them trying to detain the person with the dog so they could be held accountable. Later that week, signs appeared on trees on the street inviting anybody who knew the departed cat to gather outside the family’s home for drinks. My flatmate and I looked at this sign and became anxious that nobody would go. I was moved almost to tears at the image of this grieving family, including two young children, with their trestle table of prosecco and nobody to serve it to.

We needn’t have worried. Dozens of people showed up, with flowers and wine and stories of giving little pieces of chicken to the cat. At this memorial, I looked around and thought: God, it is actually quite strange and perhaps reflects poorly on all of us that most of us had never met. Our street, as far as I know, had no WhatsApp group. If it had done, I would have known these people already. Community, especially in big cities, can be hard to come by, and is precious to people when it’s found. After that cat memorial, we invited two of our newfound neighbours over for drinks. We’ve since become friends. I felt, for the first time, part of my local area.

Neighbourhood WhatsApp groups can be a way to create that feeling. But. But! They are also places where people exercise their worst small-time cop impulses, demonstrate their smallmindedness, allow the little annoyances of life to induce them to send people they hardly know crazed screeds about recycling etiquette. Would you give up the latter if you had to give up the former as well, though?

Here’s a comment Dave Ward, Ring’s managing director of international, gave to the Guardian about what they want to do. “We are going to coach people to make sure they’re creating the right sort of post, asking them if that’s really something they want to write or whether it really needs that descriptive term, to help stop the type of content no one wants to see and make it more community focused. That’s very different to other places [such as WhatsApp groups].”

So Ring wants to streamline things, moderate, vet, polish. I have worked my way around to feeling, however, that the problem here isn’t just Ring wanting to connect us all up to the police, encouraging the darker side of local message groups, that micro-nation surveillance state tendency, or even it wanting to induct more people into local groups that can so often be irritating. It’s that the rough edges of these groups are the spice of life. You don’t have to participate in a neighbourhood WhatsApp group, but if you choose to be in one, the price for the moments of kindness and connection you can find within them is the nonsense.

Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist

editorials.title: Look again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right success
editorials.passage:
G ermany held three regional elections this month and, although each of them had a unique result, much of the media and political commentary reduced them to: “ German chancellor clings to power after latest loss to far right . Since 2016, the year of Brexit and Trump, “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” has become the overarching narrative about Europe. But while these elections were important, this reductive take both oversimplifies the complexities of contemporary European politics and drives a defeatist “ end of democracy ” narrative.

Saxony-Anhalt’s election on 6 September was a global news event – understandably, given Germany’s history, economy and place in Europe. The international media had speculated for months about an outright majority for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party came close, setting a record score with 43.8%, but it has so far failed to form a government, despite the amenable position of the “left-conservative” Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.

Two weeks later, the AfD came in first again, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, with 38.2% of the vote. International media interest was much less pronounced this time, maybe because it was the second of the three ballots, but more likely because the party was not close to reaching a majority. Moreover, the far-right success was overshadowed by the dramatic defeat for the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. For the first time in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany , the party did not make it into a state parliament. The relatively modest loss of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD), on the other hand, was barely discussed.

Finally, in the Berlin state election on the same day, the Left party (Die Linke) scored a stunning victory, gaining almost twice as many new votes as the AfD, which came in only third. Berlin will most likely now be governed by a Left-Greens-SPD coalition, headed by Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish political refugees. Perhaps most striking was that a clear majority of young women ( 54% ) voted for the “far-left” party, representing a broader leftwing trend among young women that continues to be ignored by most media and politics representatives.

Whereas the Saxony-Anhalt election was often generalised as the story of Germany , if not Europe as a whole , the Berlin election is, at best, flattened out to a story of capital cities: uniquely cosmopolitan metropoles inhabited by highly educated progressives and immigrants. No matter that Saxony-Anhalt’s population, at 2.1 million, is just slightly over half the size of Berlin’s, and is among the oldest and whitest in the country. Moreover, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a state that is much more like Saxony-Anhalt than like Berlin, will most likely also be governed by a Left-Left-Green government – a striking fact that again has gone largely undiscussed.

This is not to say that the success of the far right and the defeat of the established parties in Germany are not important or alarming, but they are not the only notable features of these elections. Actually, the fact that two of the three states will have leftwing governments is in many ways more newsworthy, given that purely leftwing governments are increasingly rare in Europe. On a similar note, global media attention on Sweden waned as soon as it was clear that the left bloc was likely to succeed in creating a new government and the far-right Sweden Democrats would not enter the government.

Reducing the many complexities of contemporary politics to an “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” narrative is not only problematic because it ignores significant other developments; notably, important transformations within major cities, where multicultural electorates are moving left rather than right (seen recently in, among others, Copenhagen and New York ). But more importantly, and dangerously, it also strengthens the far-right’s populist narrative, which portrays politics as a struggle between “the elite” (that is, all the mainstream parties) and “the people” (allegedly represented by the far right).

Similarly, some media have been keen to adopt the “horseshoe” theory of politics , prominently and strategically used by Merz , in which the liberal-democratic mainstream is squeezed from both sides, by the far right and far left. This conflates two very different challenges though. While it is true that established parties are challenged by new(er) parties, particularly because younger voters vote less for the established right and left, this includes liberal democratic parties like the Greens, too.

Moreover, while the far right does threaten liberal democracy – and the AfD even threatens democracy per se – the so-called far left rarely does. Like Die Linke, most parties that are considered “far left” are former communist parties which have become significantly more moderate over time, presenting an ideology that reflects the social democracy of the 1970s much more than the revolutionary socialism of the former communist world. In fact, few “far left” parties are still even populist these days.

So, while both the far right and “far left” threaten the established parties, only the far right threatens liberal democracy. It makes political sense for established politicians such as Merz to equate liberal democracy with the established parties, but the media should not uncritically share these claims. Surveys continue to show evidence of what the US political scientist Robert Dahl termed “ a democratic paradox ”: where very high support for the system of democracy is combined with very high dissatisfaction with the state of real, existing democracy.

By highlighting the complexities of contemporary politics, in particular the frustration of the young (women) who are looking for liberal democratic alternatives to established parties, both the far-right populist binary of “establishment versus far right” and the defeatist “end of democracy” narrative are weakened. Hopefully this will give space to liberal democratic parties, old and new, to move beyond the self-defeating strategy of catering again and again to the same stereotypical voter with “legitimate concerns” , and instead mobilise and represent different groups of dissatisfied democrats.

Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author of The Far Right Today

editorials.title: The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
editorials.passage:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States came with all the choreography: a B-2 flyover, pandas, a Nixon-era toast. But for anyone watching from the Global South, the spectacle was beside the point. More important was Beijing’s emphasis on “constructive strategic stability” in its relationship with Washington. For capitals from Riyadh to New Delhi to Jakarta, the summit offered a glimpse of how they may navigate relations with the two powers over the rest of this decade.

Beijing emerged from the summit offering diplomatic cover without military entanglement. Washington, by contrast, came to the meeting already embroiled in the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war on Iran, pressing allies on trade, reasserting US dominance in Latin America, and demanding that the Global South choose sides in its effort to contain China, all while Trump himself toasted Xi and hailed the summit as a success. For governments across the Global South being urged to distance themselves from Beijing, that contrast will not go unnoticed.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the Gulf. Trump wants China, Tehran’s largest trading partner, to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, choked since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February. Xi backed a return to a ceasefire and eventual peace talks, but the Chinese readout offered no specifics on reopening the strait and no commitment to pressure Iran. Beijing appears determined to preserve its room for manoeuvre.

For Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Doha, that has obvious advantages. China can call Tehran, issue a UN statement, or offer to mediate, all without deploying a single soldier or demanding a military base. Meanwhile, Washington is a direct party to the war, and its credibility as a security guarantor is eroded by the very crisis it helped create. Gulf capitals are already calibrating: stay under the US umbrella for hardware, but hedge through Beijing for diplomatic crisis management and energy-market stability. China’s usefulness, in other words, lies partly in the fact that it is not fighting the wars Washington is.

That calculation extends across the wider region. For Iraq, Egypt and Algeria, all watching energy prices spike and shipping lanes choke, China’s restraint has its appeal. The Global South does not need another great power to join the war; it needs someone who can talk to all sides without shooting. Beijing is positioning itself to play that role.

For governments elsewhere across the Global South, this creates a difficult set of choices. They are pressed to distance themselves from China, even as Trump himself re-engages. They are asked to absorb tariffs and supply-chain shocks, while Washington and Beijing extend their own trade truce for another two months. The result is a growing sense that other countries are expected to bear the costs of great-power rivalry while Washington and Beijing retain the freedom to negotiate with each other.

The response is already visible. India deepens its multipolar balancing, buying Russian oil while courting US tech and Chinese investment. Indonesia continues its “free and active” foreign policy, signing defence deals with both Washington and Beijing. South Africa and Brazil use BRICS platforms to hedge, not as anti-Western gestures but as insurance against a system where others write the rules. The summit did not cause this hedging, but it is likely to reinforce it.

Artificial intelligence raises a different problem for the Global South: who gets to set the rules. Xi’s emphasis on “human control” and Trump’s resistance to new AI guardrails represent two competing visions, but neither was designed with the interests of countries across the Global South at its centre. The two sides have agreed to continue a new AI dialogue and are discussing an incident-notification mechanism, but no binding rules exist. Many countries will remain dependent on AI systems, infrastructure and standards developed elsewhere, with little say over the norms that govern them. China’s state-led model may look more attractive than America’s corporate-led alternative, but it is still another form of dependence.

Yet the Global South is not entirely passive. India is building indigenous large language models and exporting its digital-public-infrastructure playbook; the United Arab Emirates has positioned itself as a major AI hub; the African Union is pushing data-sovereignty frameworks aimed at giving African states greater control over their data and digital infrastructure. These efforts are nascent but show a determination to avoid a simple choice between US and Chinese models. Beijing has tried to institutionalise its vision, launching a Global AI Governance Initiative and helping establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, whose founding agreement was signed by 29 countries in Shanghai in July. For some, this offers an alternative to Western frameworks; for others, it swaps one dependency for another. The question is whether countries across the Global South can coordinate strongly enough to shape the rules themselves.

Beyond the ceremony, the broader message from the summit is already clear. Washington secured the photographs and a temporary tariff truce; Beijing secured something more strategic: recognition of the terms on which it wants the relationship managed. For governments across the Global South, the meeting reinforced an approach many are already pursuing: avoid choosing sides where possible, maintain ties with both powers and use the competition between them to preserve room for manoeuvre.

Great-power rivalry, on Beijing’s terms, is not peace. But for capitals from Riyadh to Jakarta, the space between Washington and Beijing can also create opportunities to build leverage and pursue their own interests. The challenge is to ensure that future deals between the two powers do not leave everyone else simply absorbing the consequences.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: What explains the recent wave of protests at the IITs?
editorials.passage:
On September 18, 2026, Sahil Wakode, a BTech student from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay died by suicide. Wakode’s parents have alleged that their son faced casteist harassment from a professor on campus.

Students mounted protests after the suicide and submitted an 18-point memorandum to the institution, demanding a fair investigation and better support systems for students.

After three days of protests, media outlets reported that the institute’s director signed the memorandum, indicating that the demands would be considered. On September 24, the institute announced that a ten-member committee would investigate the incident.

The previous month, IIT Delhi had also seen protests after the death by suicide of a student, named Rishikesh Kumar. The institution’s students demanded that an external inquiry committee be formed, and that the student’s family be compensated, and also called for broader policy changes.

The students paused their protests after six days, after the institution formed the committee – Kumar’s parents declined compensation.

Many students told Scroll that the protesting IIT students had been inspired by the protest launched by the Cockroach Janata Party in July. “There are student protests happening all over the country so, even we felt emboldened to raise our issues,” said one student from IIT Bombay. “For the first time, we are seeing that protests can actually be impactful and I think students also feel like they can make demands for a better life.” All those who spoke to Scroll requested anonymity because they feared retribution from their institutions.

Nevertheless, the intensity of the protests was striking, given that the IITs have not typically been known as sites of student politics.

A key reason for this is institutional opposition to such activities. In 2023, IIT Bombay explicitly stated in its rules and regulations that all protests, including marches, and gathering on campuses “require prior permission from the institute and the local police”.

The institution also warned students against speaking to “the press, media persons, or any external agencies on any matters related to the Institute without prior approval from authorized Institute officials”. The rules also state that students cannot “post, share, or disseminate any false information related to the Institute on social media platforms” and that “unauthorized sharing of confidential or sensitive Institute matters on social media is strictly prohibited”.

The institution enforced these rules in 2025, and suspended a student for allegedly making “unauthorised comments” to the media. He was reinstated after approaching a court, which ruled in his favour. The professor who headed the disciplinary committee that decided on the suspension is the same one named in the recent incident.

IITs have also restricted political activities in specific circumstances. Earlier this year, during the Cockroach Janata Party protests, for instance, IIT Rourkee asked students and faculty to refrain from political activity without seeking the institution’s permission.

Similarly, in 2020, as protests against the Constitutional Amendment Act played out, the IIT Bombay director told students to keep politics off campus. In 2018, IIT Kharagpur issued a circular banning students from “political/apolitical gathering/meeting” ahead of a planned march in support of students from Aligarh Muslim University who had been assaulted by police.

In another, earlier instance, from 2015, IIT Madras derecognised the student group Ambedkar Periyar Reading Circle – it withdrew its decision a week later, after strong protests from students across the country.

Unsurprisingly, then, student political groups like the left-leaning Student Federation of India or the right-leaning Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad have not established a presence in the IITs. In fact, IIT Madras’s rules explicitly state that students are allowed “to form associations and student organizations as long as they are not affiliated to external political parties”, or groups that “promote hatred”.

But faculty and students noted that in the absence of forums in which to speak up, frustrations over several problems have been building up in recent years. These include inadequate infrastructure, social isolation and uncertain job prospects.

One faculty member observed that securing a seat at an IIT is an immensely difficult task, and that most students spend several years and several lakhs of rupees at coaching centres to be able to crack the entrance exams. “After all that, they come to the institutions to find out that there are even more struggles here,” they said. “The institutions don’t match up to the students’ expectations.”

The IIT Madras student noted that student suicides become “flashpoints” for unrest, and that in such situations, administrations “really cannot stop the student from protesting”.

According to data compiled by Dheeraj Singh, founder of the Global IIT Alumni Support group and an alumnus of IIT Kanpur, in the last 10 years, 120 students have died of suicides or unnatural causes, while the the previous decade saw 51 such deaths. The data also showed that Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students died by suicide at roughly two times higher rates than general category students.

Since 2023, a total of eight students have died by suicide in IIT Delhi, and this year alone, three have died by suicide at IIT Bombay.

One alumnus of an IIT observed that students were frustrated with the absence of measures to tackle this problem. “Every time such a suicide happens, the administration will form such committees, show some interest in the matter and then ten days later everything goes back to normal,” they said. “We see the same thing happen every single time there is a suicide, nobody seems to be taking any concrete steps.”

The first faculty member noted that the deeper infrastructural problems that students have been frustrated about include a lack of space. In IIT Delhi, for instance, they noted, there were simply not enough classrooms to accommodate students, and hostel rooms were inadequate as well. “Students are crammed into hostel rooms, there have been issues regarding drinking water and hygiene too,” they said.

A key reason for this is that while student numbers have increased dramatically over recent years, the institutions have not been allocated sufficient additional resources. “Infrastructure has not evolved with time,” one student from IIT Delhi said. Further, the first faculty member noted that they were struggling to teach the expanded classes.

Faculty and students’ impression of IITs diminishing reputation is also reflected in their concerns over placements. While once IITs would boast of students bagging huge salary packages, the alumnus said, “That doesn’t happen any more. Students still get, but they are few.”

The first faculty member also said that students were finding it difficult to land “high salaried jobs”. According to data submitted by the Centre to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports in 2025, in 22 out of 23 IITs, placements had fallen significantly in the three years between 2021-’22 and 2023-’24. While some attribute this fall to a normalisation after a spike in hiring after the Covid-19 pandemic, recent media reports indicate that securing jobs did, indeed, remain a challenge.

“The image of IITs being this prestigious institute that guarantees a secure future is being shattered,” the alumnus said. “In the last few years, the institution is not releasing placement data.”

At the same time, the fees at the institutions have also seen significant hikes in recent years. In 2022, students of IIT Bombay held a month-long protest against a fee hike of 39% for MTech students and 45% for PhD students. The institution partially rolled back the fees after the protests.

“Students are forced to take loans to pay their fees and after that if they are graduating with loans and not a good job, then that causes a lot of stress,” the first faculty member said. “Both to the student and the parents.”

Students also decried what they said was an increasingly restrictive environment on IIT campuses. “There is such high security everywhere. There’s a running joke that entering our campus is like going to the airport,” another IIT Bombay student said. “We see people in uniforms all over campus.”

She added, “There are also several places on campus that are now forbidden, there are so many rules regarding every single thing. It has become suffocating. All of these reasons combined is what is causing so much frustration among students.”

The IIT Madras student explained that though their campus had a wide range of clubs, students could not have free conversations within them. “The administration assigns a professor to each of these clubs, and I think this is because they want to keep an eye on what we are up to,” he said. “So, students feel like they are being watched and there is no space to discuss issues.”

The IIT Bombay student also argued that the attitude of many faculty members was outdated. They see the teacher-student relationship as “purely transactional”, she said, an approach that had “reached its limit and is now crashing and burning”.

The first faculty member noted that the challenges students face are particularly acute for those from Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Class communities – these students often have to take loans to enroll in the institutions, and once they arrive on campuses, find themselves isolated from other students. “Even general category students find it hard to feel a sense of belonging, so obviously it is worse for students from marginalised backgrounds,” they said. “It is very difficult for them to navigate these spaces.”

That marginalised students find themselves in an oppressive environment was apparent from the tenor of some public conversations that followed Wokade’s death – for instance, rather than consider the allegation of casteist harassment that his family had raised, some social media users scrutinised CCTV footage of the exam to determine whether or not he had cheated in the exam.

The second faculty member also noted that the professor in question received a groundswell of support from faculty from IIT Bombay, IIT Delhi, IIT Madras and other IITs after the family raised the matter of caste. “After the family invoked the SC/ST atrocity act, immediately everyone came to the defence of the professor,” the faculty member pointed out. “Until then everyone was protesting.”

Further, some argued that support systems on the campuses for distressed students were inadequate. “Students don’t find the counselors to be good and prefer to get a reference from the campus hospital to go see therapists outside the campus,” the second IIT Bombay student said.

This difficulty is compounded by the intense competition within the institutions, and a view that prevails among many students who perform poorly or do not graduate simply could not cope with the pressure. “By design, life in an IIT is isolating, even spaces within the campus are designed in a way to prevent proper socialisation among students,” the student said. “Everybody on the outside thinks that life in IIT is perfect but it really isn’t.”

Are the recent agitations then an indication of a shift on IIT campuses, and of an increasing politicisation of the institutions’ students?

Conversations with students and faculty members from four IITs suggest that this is not the case. The first student from IIT Bombay said that she had observed that the initiative to start a protest was taken by students with “some political leanings” but that as the protests grew, so did demands to ensure they remained apolitical. “There have been protests and marches in the past as well,” she said. “Students will come together for some issues, but even in this one, they said they don’t want it to get political. Even though all things are political.”

A student of IIT Madras said he felt that “‘politics’ is kind of a bad word” in the institutions. “But I feel that there is a kind of awareness that is also emerging among the students,” he said. “Probably because the peer groups are also changing, thanks to diverse students from different backgrounds and socio-economic background students who are coming into the campuses.”

Many protesting students, however, worried that unrest would damage the institution’s name, the IIT Bombay student observed. “They may voice out issues but they don’t want the issues to get out and for the institution’s reputation to be affected,” she said. “They don’t see themselves as separate from the institution and so don’t want the institution to be criticised.”

In fact, one professor from an IIT said that in the protests in Mumbai, they had observed some students raising slogans against party-affiliated student groups like the Students Federation of India. “They want their protests to be ‘pure’, they seem to view student politics that happen in other campuses as ‘dirty’,” the professor said. “And they seem to not want these protests to be tainted by that kind of politics.”

editorials.title: Ramachandra Guha’s new book: Gandhi’s nonviolence prepared Indians to use their freedom responsibly
editorials.passage:
In the past, the argument that Gandhi’s reliance on non-violence delayed the country’s freedom from British rule was put forward most insistently by Marxists, themselves enchanted with the examples of Lenin and Mao. More recently, the ideas that non-violence was a bogus and ineffective strategy has become widespread among Indians who are not remotely attached to Marxism. Those who argue that the struggle against British rule should have relied largely or exclusively on violence make two claims – first, that freedom would then have come sooner than 1947; and second, that a legacy of successful armed struggle against colonialism would have led to a more realistic, hard-headed, and effective foreign policy for the nation once it was independent. Gandhi, and the Gandhian legacy, are charged with weakening the Indian people in their fight against Western imperialism as well as with undermining the Indian nation’s ability to become a major player in global affairs.

The Tamil novelist and public intellectual D Jeyamohan has persuasively challenged the belief that violent revolution would have led the British to depart sooner, or resulted in a better and stronger India. Before Gandhi returned to India, he remarks, “some ‘intellectuals’ believed that the British could be driven out using violent means.” After Gandhi died, he continues, “the naxalites too shared the same belief and modus operandi.”

Jeyamohan provides a critical assessment of the three proponents of armed struggle who so enchant younger Indians today. Of Savarkar, Bhagat Singh, and Subhas Chandra Bose he writes that “their rebellion was a childish effort completely based on their belief in violence and a misbegotten sense of personal adventure. Their misplaced confidence came from imagining themselves to be extraordinary men capable of determining history. Essentially, it stemmed from a lack of faith in the great power of the people.”

On the other hand, notes Jeyamohan, Gandhi “meticulously avoided violence at every turn”. His principled adherence to non-violence was coupled with a refusal to demonise the white rulers. This was because “his struggle was for the basic democratic rights of Indians and was not a war against the British.”

Using the methods pioneered by Gandhi to free itself from British rule, independent India became a multi-party democracy. What might have happened if more violent methods had been resorted to instead? Here is Jeyamohan’s verdict: “In my view, India would have been led to annihilation if any of these three men – VD Savarkar, Bhagat Singh, or Subhash Chandra Bose – had won popular support and come to power. Through their misapprehension of history, they would have caused the same devastation wreaked by Ayatollah Khomeini, Josef Stalin, and Adolf Hitler respectively in their own nations.”

Jeyamohan’s essay was published in the summer of 2023. More than half a century previously, the case for Gandhi’s non-violence had been made with equal vigour by the eminent British liberal John Grigg. Writing in the Sunday Times to mark the centenary of Gandhi’s birth, Grigg accepted that freedom may have come sooner to India through other means. Had Gandhi not stopped the Non-Cooperation movement after the violence at Chauri-Chaura in 1922, a multiplication of such incidents might have destroyed the Raj. That, for Gandhi, would not have meant an independence worth winning. By insisting on non-violence, and hastening slowly, Gandhi prepared Indians for using their freedom with greater responsibility when it eventually came.

Had Gandhi not been in their way, preaching non-violence and successfully persuading Indians to eschew violence, the likes of Bhagat Singh, Savarkar and Bose might possibly have liberated India from the British more quickly. Gandhi may have delayed formal political freedom for his fellow Indians, but, writes Grigg, in doing so he “achieved incalculable success in liberating them from themselves. No other national leader has given his people such an education in the higher forms of patriotism and citizenship. Even his cult of the spinning-wheel, though no answer to India’s economic problems, was of immense psychological value as an antidote to apathy and a unifying discipline. By his denunciation of caste and communal barriers, his assertion of women’s rights, and his emphasis on personal self-control as the necessary precondition of political self-government, he made Indian nationalism the most constructive force of its kind in history”.

… In 1957, the Vietnamese independence hero Ho Chi Minh came to India on a state visit. He was taken to Gandhi’s memorial in Delhi, where he remarked that, like other anti-colonial leaders in Asia and Africa, he had been inspired by the leader of India’s freedom struggle. An official English translation has him saying: “I and others may be revolutionaries, but we are all followers of Mahatma Gandhi, whether directly or indirectly”. This much is recorded; but folklore has it that Ho added that had Gandhi been fighting the French, he would have given up non-violence within a week.

This addendum may be apocryphal, though George Orwell, who followed Indian affairs closely and briefly served as a police officer under the Raj, likewise insisted that Gandhi’s methods could only have worked against the British . “It is difficult to see”, wrote Orwell, “how his [Gandhi’s] strategy of fasting and civil disobedience could be applied in a country where political opponents simply disappear and the public never hears anything that the Government does not want it to hear”.

The great German-American political theorist Hannah Arendt held views similar to those of Ho and Orwell. In what may be the only reference to Gandhi in her rich and varied oeuvre, she writes: “If Gandhi’s enormously powerful and successful strategy of nonviolent resistance had met with a different enemy – Stalin’s Russia, Hitler’s Germany, even prewar Japan, instead of England – the outcome would not have been decolonisation, but massacre and submission”.

There could have been no Gandhi in Arendt’s native Germany, but in her adoptive country there was Martin Luther King, whose campaigns she was surely acquainted with. Though disfigured by inequality and oppression, the United States of the 1950s and 1960s was, like the British India of the 1920s and 1930s, far from being what Arendt (in her most famous work) characterised as a “totalitarian” society. For all its harshness and lack of justice, it still had some spaces open for negotiation, dialogue, and moral growth. These were adroitly exploited by King and his comrades. For, as the historian Harvard Sitkoff has noted, “King’s neo-Gandhian persuasion fit the needs of the American South in the mid-20th century. …He clothed the consequences of racial change in the garb of reconciliation and the creation of a beloved community. At the least, this disarming message from a man of God minimised virulent white opposition and made the inevitable appear a bit more acceptable”.

The totalitarian regime erected by Hitler in Germany – from which Arendt herself was an exile – was finally crushed only through the massed military might of the Allied Forces. However, the Soviet Empire erected by Stalin in Russia and thereafter across all of Eastern Europe did not fall as a result of a Third World War. One reason for its collapse was the self-awareness of Mikhail Gorbachev, who realised that the system he headed had to reform. A second was the subtle – and not so subtle – pressure exercised by the Soviet Union’s rival superpower, the United States. A third, which we focus on below, consisted of resistance movements within the countries of Eastern Europe which absolutely eschewed the use of violence.

The most salient example here is that of Solidarity, the trade union movement that challenged the Polish Communist state, and in doing so, provided a worthy example for citizens of other countries in the Soviet bloc to emulate. In 1989, Poland held its first free election. Eighteen years later, the iconic Solidarity leader Lech Walesa came to India for an international conference on non-violence. He told an interviewer in Mumbai that “we failed when we tried to combat Communism with weapons, but when we took up Mahatma Gandhi’s tactics and strategy, we emerged winners.”

Walesa may have been flattering his hosts. As a workers’ leader in Poland, he had innovated his tactics on the spot, rather than taking clues from the ideas of a long-dead Indian. But that Gandhi was indeed an influence on Solidarity is confirmed by a key document dating from the days of the struggle. This is a letter written from Gdansk Prison in 1985 by a major participant in the Polish movement for democracy, the writer Adam Michnik.

Gandhi was also significant to other dissidents who played important roles in bringing democracy to Poland, though without garnering the international reputations of Wałęsa or Michnik. A priest named Father Ludwik Wiśniewski organised “Social Concern Weeks” from the early 1980s, in which opposition figures from across Poland participated. In these camps, Gandhian philosophy, “a theme important to Father Ludwik”, was regularly discussed. Writers in the Polish underground press spoke of the relevance of Gandhi and his techniques of nonviolent civil disobedience to their own situation. Meanwhile, in Hungary, young activists had formed a “Peace Group for Dialogue” in 1982. Through the rest of the decade, they held a series of camps and meetings, where the ideas and legacies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King were debated. In this manner, for the philosophically-minded dissidents who later led or participated in the non-violent revolutions of 1989, “reading Gandhi was their answer to those who preached Lenin.”

Among those who have testified to Gandhi’s influence on himself and his mates is the leading Czech dissident Jan Urban. In 1987, the Government of Czechoslovakia allowed the screening of Richard Attenborough’s Oscar-winning film, Gandhi . This, as Urban ironically put it, “was one of the most stupid mistakes the communist regime ever made”. For those who saw the film, “it was not about Gandhi and British and India. It was about us. It was about how you stand up for your dream and how you stand up for your freedom. For your rights.”

Urban saw the film several times, as did many other young Czech citizens. What the film unwittingly showed them “was this symbol of non-violence and … it became absolutely clear that in this hectic regime change violence never was an option.” People accustomed to a wearying diet of Soviet propaganda began to think of democracy and human rights. The feelings suppressed for so long burst out into art; thus “anonymous people started to draw Gandhi graffiti, you know, bald head, big ears. Round spectacles and a smile.”

When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, an East German worker told a visiting British journalist that the collapse of the Soviet Empire “shows Lenin was wrong. Lenin said a revolution could succeed only with violence, but this was a peaceful revolution”. In the three-and-a-half decades since that event, it is the methods of Gandhi rather than of Lenin that have more often inspired popular movements against authoritarian regimes across the globe. Tellingly, protests that do not rely on guns or tanks tend to have happier outcomes. One recent study estimates that, in the period since the end of the Second World War, 57% of successful non-violent campaigns against authoritarian leaders led to democracy, whereas for campaigns that relied on violence, the number was merely 6%.

Excerpted with permission from Arguments with Gandhi, Ramachandra Guha, forthcoming on October 2 from HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: Trump-Xi summit showed Indian foreign policy needs junking of shibboleths and a brutal reckoning
editorials.passage:
The contrast couldn’t be greater. Donald Trump went out of his way to shower attention and sycophancy on Xi Jinping. He broke six decades of protocol to receive the Chinese president at the airport, called him “strong, vibrant and fit”, gave him a personal tour of the White House, cutting short the all-important bilateral meeting, raised a toast to Xi and his spouse at a lavish state dinner, gifted him an ornate bald eagle statuette and declared: “As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better.”

His administration, meanwhile, extended the ‘Busan trade truce’ for another two months, ensuring mutual tariff reductions. Just a few days ahead of Xi’s arrival, Trump had signed into law a bipartisan bill that gave the US president the authority to slap a 100% tariff on the biggest purchasers of Russian oil, a list where China sits comfortably on top. Yet none in the administration, and certainly not Trump, was even thinking about penalising China and implementing the Lindsey O Graham Russia Sanctions Act.

Instead, Trump treated Xi with fawning flattery far in excess of what he had received in Beijing in May, kept the $14 billion Taiwan arms package in suspension, ignored questions from American reporters on Taiwan and sought to ingratiate himself to curry favour with the Chinese president in terms so endearing that they left even his Republican Party members squirming in discomfort.

Around the same time, India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar was in New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly proceedings. He found time to meet the US secretary of state Marco Rubio and flagged India’s pressing concerns over the new US law to punish Russia’s energy buyers.

Since we have only the official statements of the interaction between the two sides, here’s what the US State Department released in its version of the meeting: “Secretary Rubio and Minister Jaishankar also exchanged views on developments in the Middle East and beyond. The two also discussed sanctions that could be leveled against states that engage economically with Russia and Iran. The Secretary emphasized that the United States remains well-positioned to help regional partners address their energy security challenges.”

Translation: Rubio told the Indian foreign minister that India must reduce its Russian oil intake or face punitive steps. This is a Hobson’s choice, since India can ill afford to reject Russian oil or allow its exports to become thoroughly uncompetitive.
On being reminded perhaps that India needs to ensure energy security for its 1.4 billion people, Rubio’s ostensible suggestion was for India to buy more American oil and gas. To the question of what it does to India’s macroeconomic stability — considering that discounted Russian Urals are invaluable for India, which imports 90% of its energy needs and is grappling with a sharp rise in global crude prices — the readout is unclear, but I wouldn’t be surprised if India’s concern was met with a shrug.

This is where we are at. Trump is seeking a “G2” condominium with China, a point that was abundantly clear as he leaned heavily on personal chemistry over substantial policy discussions and serious summitry, frequently praised Xi and Peng Liyuan as “truly outstanding, amazing people” and described his bond with the Chinese president as a “truly great friendship”.

All pressing issues were swept aside — a bargain China would settle readily for. The visit produced no announced breakthrough on the hardest disputes — trade, Taiwan, Artificial Intelligence or Iran. Its clearest message was that Washington wants to keep the contest with Beijing manageable and the relationship negotiable.
Trump was never a China hawk, but in his first term was hemmed in by Washington’s China hawks.

By appointing a bunch of spineless sycophants to his Cabinet this time, Trump has ensured a freer hand in his second term and a lot more space to assert himself. Alongside, US attitudes, especially among the younger generation of Americans, have considerably warmed towards Beijing.

In line with his innate belief in striking ‘deals’ with a peer competitor and an industrial powerhouse, Trump’s signalling towards China since he assumed office for the second time — and reinforced during Xi’s state visit to the US — has been one of unilateral concessions, be it relaxing advanced semiconductor restrictions, extending tariff relief, respecting China’s red lines on Taiwan or using Taiwan as a ‘negotiating chip’. He is genuinely in awe of Xi’s power, authority and control.

That poses problems for India. For over two decades, the US-India relationship was framed by rhetoric emphasising ‘democratic solidarity’. From Kurt Campbell to Marco Rubio (even in Trump’s second term), policymakers consistently described the partnership as the “defining relationship of the 21st century”, bound by ‘shared values’ and a commitment to an open regional order.

Now Rubio is describing US-China relations in these exact terms.
In a way, it is good that the rhetoric on “values” and “democracy” has been done away with. India should actually be thankful to Trump for showing how power behaves without the mask. When the US president spoke about power in such naked terms, I had expected the Washington establishment to push back hard against the decimation of the order the US itself helped build and now finds inconvenient. Except for a few honourable mentions, it is apparent that the Washington establishment not only agrees with Trump; it is happy that Trump has made America’s position clear.

That’s THE tectonic shift. America’s treaty allies such as Europe and Canada, and partners such as India, are only now grasping the true gamut of the change. This is also an inflection point and a brutal reckoning for India’s foreign policy, and it calls for a complete reset of our ties with the US.

The zero-sum triangle of the India-US-China equation holds that American accommodation of Beijing is a potential reduction in Washington’s commitment to balancing Chinese power in the Indo-Pacific, which in turn reduces India’s usefulness. This is causing profound disquiet in New Delhi.

This anxiety should be the starting point for a derisking and diversification of India’s foreign policy, which has come to adopt an axiomatic belief that American security, capital, technology and markets are indispensable for our rise.

If Washington is no longer interested in helping India develop its capabilities, if it sees in India the rise of a third pole and another potential peer competitor and is therefore implementing extractive policies to cope with its own decline anxieties, then persistent calls for attaching ourselves as an appendage to a reluctant America amount to vassalage and willing acceptance of neocolonialism.

Our elites in strategic affairs should wake up and smell the Americano.
Under the arithmetic of the ‘America First’ doctrine, the Trump administration has pivoted towards siphoning economic and strategic gains from allies and partners as it grapples with the loss of its relative advantage.

For instance, Rubio says, “the United States will always act, as long as President Trump is in office, in the national interest of our country, not in the interest of the international order.”

What he left unsaid is that Washington finds the international order that it itself built to maintain primacy now unsuitable and inadequate, and wants allies and partners to contribute more to compensate for its relative decline.

When a superpower panics over losing its global edge, it becomes more transactional, forcing friends and partners to prop up its primacy at their own expense. Any partner that prioritises its own national interests over Washington’s faces penalties. India is simply the latest country to experience this squeeze, more so because it is unable to impose costs on Washington comparable to those Beijing can wield across trade and supply chains.

Unsurprisingly, Trump’s policy towards India has become nakedly extractive, aimed at yielding immediate, measurable benefits. Instead of allowing India the strategic autonomy to manage its own energy and defence matrices, Washington has used geopolitical crises to force New Delhi into compliance.

Judged purely through an ‘America First’ lens, this coercive approach has yielded substantial economic and strategic dividends for the US, as Kriti Upadhyaya points out on X.

In the economic sphere, India absorbed US protectionist levies without retaliating. New Delhi lowered its own tariffs, eased regulatory frictions and banned so-called ‘forced-labour’ imports to satisfy Washington. This compliance contributed to a 21% surge in US exports to India. India paused a stringent amendment to the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) by routing it to a parliamentary panel following American pressure. Indian corporations pledged a historic $20.5 billion in investments at the SelectUSA summit, marking the largest commitment ever made by a single country in the programme’s history.

US pressure repeatedly compelled India to scale back its purchases of discounted Russian crude, replacing these volumes with American LNG and LPG. India has continued to fund the US defence-industrial base. Yet, despite these concessions, Washington has maintained tariff threats, pressured India’s sovereign energy choices and crossed historical red lines regarding Pakistan.

The larger danger, however, is that the “G2” posture will outlive Trump. A future US administration could conclude that US-China competition should be managed through direct bargaining because escalation against a peer competitor carries unacceptable economic and security costs.

Public attitudes could make such a turn easier. Americans, especially younger ones, are increasingly warming to the Chinese, while Indian-Americans are facing surging racism in the US.

Washington may still compete with China, but it will seek to manage the relationship through “constructive strategic stability”. For India, that would mean even narrower strategic space as well as more pressure to deliver concessions.
I’d like to end by stressing that though there has been a torrent of advice on what India should, or should not, do, a distinction needs to be made between what the Indian state knows it must do and what it can do under prevailing circumstances.

Indian policymakers and even politicians are hyper-realists on the world stage. However, while realism tells us that we need to be stronger, more capable, and increase our economic growth and military and technological capabilities exponentially, we lack the wherewithal to do so at a pace we would like to. Hence, the best possible option is to somehow punch above our weight.

This is becoming increasingly difficult in a multipolar world. Our core problem, however, is dysfunctional domestic politics. As long as these impulses pull India in different directions, India will never be able to meet its objectives. The prescription of derisking and diversifying our foreign policy, therefore, should be preceded by internal balancing, domestic reforms, constructive politics at home and a ruthless pursuit of leverage. There is no other objective worth pursuing.
